summary.text: The addition principle, or rule of sum, is a basic counting principle in combinatorics.
If one thing can be done in A ways and another in B ways, and both cannot be done at the same time, there are A + B ways to choose one.
In terms of sets, for two sets with no elements in common, the size of their union equals the sum of their sizes.

facts.label: Condition
facts.value: The two actions cannot be done at the same time

facts.label: Set form
facts.value: For disjoint sets, the union's size is the sum of sizes

facts.label: Shopping example
facts.value: 3 shops in the north plus 2 in the south gives 5

facts.label: More sets
facts.value: It extends to several pairwise disjoint sets

items.prompt: Dev will go home today by either one of 3 bus routes or one of 2 tram routes, never both. How many different ways home does he have?

options.label: 6 ways
1 way
5 ways
32 ways

items.explain: He takes only one kind of route, so the ways add: 3 + 2 = 5.

items.prompt: Dev takes either a bus or a tram home, with 3 bus routes and 2 tram routes. Why is the number of ways not 3 × 2?

options.label: He uses only one of the two, so the counts add instead
Because 3 × 2 is too large to be a real count
Because trams and buses use different numbers of stops
Because multiplying only works for even numbers

items.explain: Multiplying counts doing both actions. When the two cannot both be done, the ways to choose one are added.

items.prompt: You count everyone in a choir and a band by adding the two member counts. For that sum to be right, what must be true?

options.label: Both groups must have the same number of members
The choir must be the larger of the two groups
Each group must have an even number of members
Nobody can belong to both groups

items.explain: The sizes add only for disjoint sets, which have no elements in common. A person in both groups would be counted twice.

items.prompt: A class has some students who walk to school and the rest who do not. Why does taking the walkers away from the whole class give the number of the rest?

options.label: Because walkers are always the smaller group
The two groups share no one and together make up the class
Because subtraction is easier than counting directly
Because the rest must be counted twice

items.explain: The walkers and the rest do not overlap, so by the addition principle their sizes add up to the class size.

items.prompt: A bookshop has fiction, cookbook and travel shelves, and no book sits on two shelves. How do you find the total number of books?

options.label: Multiply the three shelf counts
Take the largest shelf count
Add the three shelf counts
Add two shelf counts and ignore the third

items.explain: The addition principle extends to several pairwise disjoint sets: the size of the union is the sum of the sizes.

items.prompt: A teacher says another basic counting rule can itself be proven using the rule of sum. Which rule is it?

options.label: The rule that order never matters
The rule that subtraction undoes addition
The rule that sets can never overlap
The multiplication principle

items.explain: The addition principle can also be used to prove the multiplication principle.
